Education only. Not for diagnosis, treatment or any clinical decision.

## In 60 seconds

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) images hydrogen nuclei, which precess in a strong magnetic field at a frequency
proportional to the field. Contrast comes from how fast their magnetization recovers after it is disturbed, the
time constant $T_1$. Gadolinium contrast agents shorten $T_1$ in proportion to their concentration, and they stay
outside cells, so tissue with more extracellular space, such as scar, ends up with a shorter $T_1$. Late gadolinium
enhancement (LGE) inverts the magnetization and reads the image when healthy myocardium has no signal: scar is
then bright [@kellman2012]. In the left atrium, fibrosis on LGE was associated with recurrence after AF ablation
[@marrouche2014], but adding ablation of that fibrosis did not reduce recurrence in a randomized trial
[@marrouche2022]. How much "fibrosis" a scan shows depends on the method and the threshold
[@boyle2022; @kamali2020]. In the ventricle, conducting channels found on LGE colocalized with functional mapping
targets [@guichard2024]. In registries of patients whose pacemakers and defibrillators were not labelled for MRI, scans
under a protocol at 1.5 T reported no long-term clinically significant adverse events [@nazarian2017].

## From the field

- **From association to trial.** In the DECAAF cohort, each 1% more atrial fibrosis on LGE was associated with
  more recurrence after AF ablation (hazard ratio 1.06), and 57 of 329 enrolled patients were excluded for poor
  image quality [@marrouche2014]. DECAAF II then randomized 843 patients with persistent AF to pulmonary vein
  isolation (PVI) with or without ablation of MRI-defined fibrosis: recurrence was 43.0% and 46.1%, not
  significantly different, with more safety events in the fibrosis-guided group [@marrouche2022]. Its lesions did
  not uniformly become scar on follow-up MRI [@akoum2024].
- **One scan, many burdens.** In 102 patients, average IIR fibrosis went from 5.0% to 37.4% of the wall as the
  threshold moved from 1.2 to 0.97; a second method agreed only modestly in space (Dice 0.49), and only that method
  predicted recurrence [@boyle2022].
- **Repeat scans.** In 45 patients scanned twice, Otsu thresholding reproduced better (Dice 71) than 3.3 standard
  deviations above the blood pool (58) or IIR above 1.61 (46); only voxels above about the 70th percentile of the
  wall histogram agreed better than chance [@kamali2020].
- **Where the threshold comes from.** In the right atrium at 3 T, the upper normal limit (mean + 2 SD in nine
  healthy volunteers) was an IIR of 1.21, and a dense-scar threshold was 1.29; agreement with voltage mapping was
  56% [@gunturiz2022].
- **Ventricular scar and channels.** In 40 patients, conducting channels found automatically on LGE were unmasked
  by deceleration zones in 78% with a double-extrastimulus mapping protocol, against 48% with baseline
  pacing [@guichard2024]. In 37 patients with nondilated left ventricular cardiomyopathy, a ring-like LGE pattern came
  with more and longer channels, and channel number and length were associated with VT recurrence
  [@pittorru2026].
- **Devices in the scanner.** At 1.5 T, 1,500 nonthoracic scans in patients with devices not labelled for MRI
  had no deaths, lead failures or losses of capture; one defibrillator not programmed per protocol had to be
  replaced [@russo2017]. In 2,103 thoracic and nonthoracic scans, nine devices (0.4%) reset to a backup mode
  [@nazarian2017]. In pigs, an LGE sequence designed for use with a defibrillator present found more heterogeneous
  tissue corridors (candidate channels), with lower specificity [@sheagren2025].

## Derivations

### Spins and the Larmor relation

A hydrogen nucleus has a magnetic moment. In a static field $B_0$ the net magnetization of many nuclei, $M_0$,
points along the field, and any part tipped away from it precesses at

$$
f = \frac{\gamma}{2\pi}\,B_0
$$ {#eq-m52-larmor}

with $\gamma/2\pi$ = 42.577 MHz/T for the proton [@codata2022]: 63.87 MHz at 1.5 T and 127.73 MHz at 3 T. An RF
pulse at this frequency tips the magnetization, and a field gradient makes the frequency depend on position, which
is how MRI encodes space (lab part A).

**Key takeaways**

- The scanner talks to protons at the Larmor frequency.
- Gradients turn frequency into position.

### Inversion recovery

After a 180° pulse the longitudinal magnetization starts at $-M_0$ and relaxes back toward $M_0$:
$dM_z/dt = (M_0 - M_z)/T_1$. Solving,

$$
M_z(t) = M_0\left(1 - 2e^{-t/T_1}\right), \qquad M_z = 0 \ \text{at}\ t = T_1 \ln 2
$$ {#eq-m52-ir}

so the signal of a tissue is zero about $0.69\,T_1$ after the inversion [@kellman2012]. Lab part B integrates the
full Bloch equations through a finite RF pulse and matches @eq-m52-ir within 1.1%, the loss to $T_2$ decay during
the pulse.

**Key takeaways**

- Each tissue crosses zero at its own time, $T_1 \ln 2$.
- Real readouts shorten the apparent $T_1$ [@kellman2012].

### Gadolinium, T1 and extracellular volume

A gadolinium agent raises the relaxation rate $R_1 = 1/T_1$ in proportion to its concentration:

$$
\frac{1}{T_1} = \frac{1}{T_{1,0}} + r_1\,[\mathrm{Gd}]
$$ {#eq-m52-relaxivity}

with relaxivity $r_1$ = 4.5 L/(mmol·s) [@kellman2012]. In Kellman and Arai's worked example, 0.15 mmol/kg in
blood that is 8% of body weight gives about 2 mmol/L in blood and 0.5 mmol/L in tissue with 25% extracellular
volume, which shortens a native $T_1$ of 950 ms to about 300 ms (lab part C). The agent stays outside cells, so a
tissue's concentration is its extracellular volume fraction (ECV) times the plasma's, and blood's is $1 - \mathrm{Hct}$
times the plasma's, where Hct is the hematocrit. Dividing the two changes in $R_1$:

$$
\mathrm{ECV} = (1 - \mathrm{Hct})\,\frac{\Delta R_{1,\text{myo}}}{\Delta R_{1,\text{blood}}}
$$ {#eq-m52-ecv}

In 26 patients with chronic infarction at 1.5 T, $T_1$ ten minutes after contrast was 379 ms in remote myocardium
and 238 ms in the infarct, with ECV 28% and 53% [@bauner2012]. The infarct's change in $R_1$ is 2.04 times the
myocardium's, close to their ECV ratio of 1.89. Scar has more room for gadolinium, so its $T_1$ falls further.

**Key takeaways**

- Gadolinium marks extracellular space, not scar as such.
- ECV turns two pairs of $T_1$ values and a hematocrit into a tissue fraction.

### Choosing the inversion time

Ignoring the readout, a magnitude LGE image shows $|1 - 2e^{-\mathrm{TI}/T_1}|$ at inversion time TI. With TI set to
null healthy myocardium ($T_{1m}\ln 2$), scar with $T_{1s} < T_{1m}$ shows $|1 - 2^{\,1 - T_{1m}/T_{1s}}|$. The signed
difference between scar and myocardium is $2(e^{-\mathrm{TI}/T_{1m}} - e^{-\mathrm{TI}/T_{1s}})$, which peaks at

$$
\mathrm{TI}^* = \frac{\ln(T_{1m}/T_{1s})}{1/T_{1s} - 1/T_{1m}}
$$ {#eq-m52-lge}

With the published means, the null is at 263 ms, scar reads 0.34 of full signal there, and $\mathrm{TI}^*$ is
298 ms (lab part D). Set TI too short and, in a magnitude image, myocardium can look brighter than scar; a
phase-sensitive reconstruction keeps the sign and is much less sensitive to TI [@kellman2012]. Blood often has an
intermediate concentration and signal, and the contrast between scar and the blood pool is frequently poor
[@kellman2012]. In our model, with an illustrative native blood $T_1$ and hematocrit, blood recovers almost as fast
as scar.

::: {.demo #m52-d1 badge="exact"}
```{=html}
<div id="m52-d1-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m52-d1"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m52-d1-inversion-time.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Model: @eq-m52-ir for an ideal inversion and an instantaneous readout, with @eq-m52-lge; tested against
  `epml.mri`.
- $T_1$ of myocardium (379 ms) and infarct (238 ms) are the published means 10 minutes after contrast at 1.5 T
  [@bauner2012]. Blood's $T_1$ (249 ms) follows from @eq-m52-ecv with an illustrative native blood $T_1$ (1600 ms)
  and hematocrit (0.42).
- What would change the result: the readout (it shortens the apparent $T_1$), time since injection, dose, field
  strength, heart rate and incomplete recovery between inversions [@kellman2012].
:::

**Key takeaways**

- The null of myocardium makes scar conspicuous; the largest difference comes a little later.
- Scar next to the blood pool can be the hardest scar to see.

### Image intensity ratio and thresholds

LGE intensities have no absolute scale; they depend on coil sensitivity, timing and dose. Atrial studies therefore
divide each wall intensity by the mean blood-pool intensity and threshold the ratio:

$$
\mathrm{IIR}_i = \frac{I_{\text{wall},i}}{\bar I_{\text{blood}}}, \qquad
B(\theta) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{1}\!\left[\mathrm{IIR}_i > \theta\right]
$$ {#eq-m52-iir}

where $B(\theta)$ is the burden: the fraction of the $N$ wall samples above the threshold $\theta$. A common gain
cancels in the ratio; the threshold does not. On our synthetic wall with 15% true fibrosis, the published thresholds
give burdens from 4.1% (IIR 1.61) to 46.2% (IIR 0.97), and no method reproduces itself perfectly on a repeat scan
(lab part E). Overlap is measured with the Dice coefficient (m40).

::: {.demo #m52-d2 badge="simulation"}
```{=html}
<div id="m52-d2-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m52-d2"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m52-d2-threshold.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Model: a synthetic, unwrapped atrial wall (60 × 120 samples) with smooth fibrotic patches covering 15% of it,
  scanned twice with independent noise, normalized by @eq-m52-iir; made by `epml.mri.synthetic_wall` with a fixed
  seed and shipped as `demos/m52-d2-wall.json`. Burden, Otsu's threshold and Dice are tested against Python.
- Normal wall has mean IIR 0.9 and SD 0.155, so that mean + 2 SD equals the published upper normal limit of 1.21,
  measured in the right atrium at 3 T [@gunturiz2022]. Patch shape, fibrotic intensity (1.5), noise and burden are
  illustrative. Thresholds are the published ones [@boyle2022; @gunturiz2022; @kamali2020].
- What it ignores: wall segmentation errors, partial volume with blood and fat, coil shading, the wall's
  thickness, and how real fibrosis is distributed.
:::

**Key takeaways**

- The reported burden is a property of the method as much as of the atrium.
- Normalization removes gain; it does not remove noise or segmentation error.

## Clinical correlate

::: {.callout-note title="Pending clinical review"}
This section describes published findings only. It is not guidance for patient care, and it has
not yet been reviewed by an EP physician.
:::

**Where MRI shows up in EP.** The cited studies use LGE to quantify atrial fibrosis before AF ablation
[@marrouche2014], to guide added ablation of fibrosis in a trial [@marrouche2022], to look at lesions after
ablation [@akoum2024], to find conducting channels in ventricular scar before VT ablation
[@guichard2024; @pittorru2026], and to scan patients with implanted devices under a protocol [@russo2017; @nazarian2017].

**What the evidence is.** The fibrosis-outcome link comes from a cohort [@marrouche2014]; the one randomized trial
of acting on it found no difference in recurrence [@marrouche2022]. Methods studies show that the number depends on
the threshold and method [@boyle2022; @kamali2020; @gunturiz2022]. The VT studies are single-center cohorts
[@guichard2024; @pittorru2026]. The device data come from prospective registries scanned at 1.5 T under protocols
[@russo2017; @nazarian2017], and the device-artifact study is in pigs [@sheagren2025].

**What a reader should ask:**

- **Which threshold and which normalization?** A burden without its method is not comparable across studies.
- **Association or intervention?** A marker that predicts recurrence is not yet a target that reduces it.
- **Which scanner, timing and protocol?** $T_1$ after contrast depends on dose, time and field strength.

## How experts think

Before trusting an LGE finding or a fibrosis number, ask:

1. **Was myocardium nulled?** A wrong TI in a magnitude image can hide scar or invent it (see
   @eq-m52-ir and @eq-m52-lge).
2. **Where is the scar relative to the blood pool?** Scar and blood can have similar $T_1$ after contrast
   [@kellman2012].
3. **What does the number depend on?** Normalization, threshold, wall segmentation and resolution
   [@boyle2022; @kamali2020].
4. **Is it reproducible?** A repeat scan is the simplest test [@kamali2020].
5. **What did the trial show?** Association is not benefit [@marrouche2014; @marrouche2022].

One sentence to keep: **LGE shows where gadolinium has room to go, read at one moment, through a threshold someone
chose.**

## Cheat sheet

| Quantity | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Larmor relation (@eq-m52-larmor) | $f = (\gamma/2\pi)B_0$; 42.577 MHz/T; 63.87 MHz at 1.5 T |
| Inversion recovery (@eq-m52-ir) | $M_z = M_0(1 - 2e^{-t/T_1})$; null at $T_1\ln 2 \approx 0.69\,T_1$ |
| Relaxivity (@eq-m52-relaxivity) | $1/T_1 = 1/T_{1,0} + r_1[\mathrm{Gd}]$; $r_1$ = 4.5 L/(mmol·s) |
| Extracellular volume (@eq-m52-ecv) | $(1 - \mathrm{Hct})\,\Delta R_{1,\text{myo}}/\Delta R_{1,\text{blood}}$ |
| Inversion time (@eq-m52-lge) | null $T_{1m}\ln 2$; scar there $|1 - 2^{1 - T_{1m}/T_{1s}}|$; peak difference at $\ln(T_{1m}/T_{1s})/(1/T_{1s} - 1/T_{1m})$ |
| Image intensity ratio (@eq-m52-iir) | $\mathrm{IIR} = I_{\text{wall}}/\bar I_{\text{blood}}$; burden = share above $\theta$ |

**Values used in this module**

| Value | Source |
| --- | --- |
| Proton $\gamma/2\pi$ = 42.577478461 MHz/T | @codata2022 |
| Relaxivity 4.5 L/(mmol·s); dose example; native myocardial $T_1$ 950 ms | @kellman2012 |
| $T_1$ after 10 minutes: myocardium 379 ms, infarct 238 ms; ECV 28% and 53% (1.5 T) | @bauner2012 |
| IIR thresholds 0.97 and 1.2 | @boyle2022 |
| IIR 1.21 upper normal and 1.29 dense scar (right atrium, 3 T) | @gunturiz2022 |

## Interview questions

Try each question before you open its model answer. In a real interview, say which assumptions you
are making.

**Q1. What frequency does a 3 T scanner transmit at, and why?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

About 127.7 MHz: the proton Larmor frequency, $(\gamma/2\pi)B_0$ with 42.577 MHz/T (@eq-m52-larmor). Only spins
precessing at that frequency respond to the RF pulse.

</details>

**Q2. Derive the null point of inversion recovery.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

$dM_z/dt = (M_0 - M_z)/T_1$ with $M_z(0) = -M_0$ gives $M_0(1 - 2e^{-t/T_1})$, which is zero at
$t = T_1\ln 2$ (@eq-m52-ir).

</details>

**Q3. Why does scar look bright on LGE?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Gadolinium stays outside cells and scar has a larger extracellular volume, so it holds more agent, its $T_1$ falls
further (@eq-m52-relaxivity), and it recovers faster after the inversion. At the TI that nulls healthy myocardium
it still has signal [@kellman2012; @bauner2012].

</details>

**Q4. Why is subendocardial scar sometimes hard to see?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Blood also holds gadolinium and can recover about as fast as scar, so the two have similar signal at the chosen TI
[@kellman2012]. In our model with illustrative blood values, blood's $T_1$ after contrast (249 ms) is close to
scar's (238 ms).

</details>

**Q5. How would you compute ECV, and what do you need?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

$T_1$ of myocardium and blood before and after contrast, and the hematocrit:
$\mathrm{ECV} = (1 - \mathrm{Hct})\,\Delta R_{1,\text{myo}}/\Delta R_{1,\text{blood}}$ (@eq-m52-ecv). It assumes the
agent has reached equilibrium between blood and tissue.

</details>

**Q6. You set TI too short on a magnitude LGE image. What happens?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Myocardium is still negative and appears with some signal; scar may be nearer zero, so contrast drops or inverts
(lab part D). Phase-sensitive reconstruction keeps the sign and is much less sensitive to TI [@kellman2012].

</details>

**Q7. Why divide atrial wall intensity by the blood pool?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

LGE intensities have no absolute scale; dividing by the blood-pool mean cancels a common gain (@eq-m52-iir). It does
not cancel noise, coil shading across the wall, or differences in blood signal from timing and dose.

</details>

**Q8. Two papers report 5% and 37% atrial fibrosis. Could it be the same patients?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Yes. In one cohort, the average IIR burden went from 5.0% to 37.4% as the threshold moved from 1.2 to 0.97
[@boyle2022]. Burden depends on the threshold and the method, so it is only comparable within one method.

</details>

**Q9. How would you test whether a fibrosis threshold is reliable?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Scan the same patients twice and measure the spatial overlap of what each scan calls fibrosis (Dice, m40);
compare methods on the same scans; and check against an independent reference such as voltage mapping. Repeat scans
favored Otsu thresholding in one study [@kamali2020]; agreement with voltage mapping was 56% in another
[@gunturiz2022].

</details>

**Q10. DECAAF found fibrosis predicted recurrence. Why did DECAAF II not show benefit from ablating it?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

A predictor is not necessarily a cause one can remove. In the trial, recurrence was 43.0% against 46.1% with no
significant difference [@marrouche2022], and the fibrosis-guided lesions did not uniformly become scar [@akoum2024].
Measurement variability (lab part E) and lesion delivery both stand between the marker and the outcome.

</details>

**Q11. What can LGE add before VT ablation?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

The extent of scar and candidate conducting channels through it. In one cohort, channels found automatically on
LGE were often unmasked by functional mapping [@guichard2024]; in another, channel number and length were associated
with recurrence [@pittorru2026]. Both are single-center studies.

</details>

**Q12. A patient has a defibrillator. What do the registries say about MRI, and what limits them?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Under protocols at 1.5 T, scans in patients with devices not labelled for MRI had no long-term clinically
significant adverse events in 2,103 scans [@nazarian2017] and no lead failures in 1,500 nonthoracic scans, with one
replacement when the protocol was not followed [@russo2017]. They are registries at one field strength under strict
protocols; the device also degrades the image, which special sequences try to address [@sheagren2025].

</details>

## Code lab

The lab goes from spins to a burden number and ends with the evidence chain.

| Part | What you do | Data |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | The Larmor frequency (@eq-m52-larmor) | CODATA 2022 |
| B | Inversion recovery from the Bloch equations (@eq-m52-ir) | our own simulation |
| C | Gadolinium, T1 and extracellular volume (@eq-m52-relaxivity, @eq-m52-ecv) | published T1 values |
| D | Choosing the inversion time (@eq-m52-lge) | published T1 values |
| E | Thresholds and burden on a synthetic wall (@eq-m52-iir) | our own phantom |
| F | Blood-pool normalization on real heart MRI | Medical Segmentation Decathlon [@antonelli2021msd] |
| G | Reading the evidence | published results |

- **Python notebook:**
  [labs/python/m52_lab.ipynb]({{< var repo.url >}}/blob/main/labs/python/m52_lab.ipynb).
  Run it from the course repository after `pip install -r requirements.txt`, or
  [open it in Google Colab]({{< var repo.colab >}}/blob/main/labs/python/m52_lab.ipynb).
- **Data:** part F downloads the Decathlon heart task once (several hundred MB, CC BY-SA 4.0), as in m40; it is
  MRI but not LGE, so it shows normalization, not fibrosis. Set `EPML_SKIP_REAL_DATA=1` to skip it. Everything
  else is published values or our own code.

Each part ends with **checks**: lines that pass with the code as given. If you change something
and a check fails, that is information, not an error to hide.

## Self-check

Short checks you can do in your head. Open each answer after you have tried it.

**S1. What is the Larmor frequency at 1.5 T, roughly?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

$42.6 \times 1.5 \approx 64$ MHz (@eq-m52-larmor).

</details>

**S2. A tissue has $T_1$ = 400 ms. When is it nulled after an inversion?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

$400 \times 0.69 \approx 277$ ms (@eq-m52-ir).

</details>

**S3. Native $T_1$ is 1000 ms and $[\mathrm{Gd}]$ = 0.4 mmol/L with $r_1$ = 4.5 L/(mmol·s). What is $T_1$?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

$1/(1 + 1.8)$ s ≈ 357 ms (@eq-m52-relaxivity).

</details>

**S4. $\Delta R_1$ is 1.5/s in myocardium and 5/s in blood, Hct 0.4. What is the ECV?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

$0.6 \times 1.5/5 = 0.18$ (@eq-m52-ecv).

</details>

**S5. A scanner's gain doubles between two scans. Does the IIR change?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

No; wall and blood both double and the ratio is unchanged (@eq-m52-iir). Noise and shading are another matter.

</details>

**S6. True or false: a higher IIR threshold always gives a lower burden.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

True for one scan: burden is the share above the threshold, which cannot grow as the threshold rises (@eq-m52-iir).
Across scans or methods, anything can happen.

</details>

## Literature figures

These figures are worth looking at alongside this module. We link to them instead of copying them:
some licenses do not allow reuse here, and others we could not confirm. Each entry says what to
look for and where this module explains it.

- **How late enhancement is made.** Kellman and Arai explain the choice of inversion time, magnitude and
  phase-sensitive reconstruction, and common artifacts, with example images and protocol tables [@kellman2012;
  [free full text](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3428749/)]. This module: choosing the inversion time.
- **Repeat scans and thresholds.** Kamali and colleagues compare four thresholding methods on scans repeated three
  months apart [@kamali2020; [free full text](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9205620/)]. This module:
  image intensity ratio and thresholds.
- **Two methods, one cohort.** Boyle and colleagues compare fibrosis maps from two methods on the same atria
  [@boyle2022; [free full text](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9911366/)]. This module: from the field.

## Further reading

- **Physics.** Late enhancement techniques [@kellman2012]; $T_1$ and ECV in infarcts [@bauner2012]; constants
  [@codata2022].
- **Atrial fibrosis.** From association to trial [@marrouche2014; @marrouche2022; @akoum2024]; methods and
  thresholds [@boyle2022; @kamali2020; @gunturiz2022].
- **Ventricular scar.** Channels and mapping [@guichard2024]; scar pattern and outcome [@pittorru2026].
- **Devices.** Registries [@russo2017; @nazarian2017]; imaging with a defibrillator present [@sheagren2025].
- **Related modules.** m40 for AI segmentation and Dice, m51 for CT anatomy, m53 for lesions and real-time MRI, m35
  for diagnostic accuracy and m45 for levels of evidence.
